  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
# Margaret's Accident

Margaret Chen had spent thirty-seven years building a reputation as a steady hand in state politics—first as a city councilwoman, then as a state representative, known for her measured responses and her ability to absorb criticism without visibly fracturing. At sixty, she had learned to move through rooms with the kind of quiet authority that came from never showing fear. But on a Tuesday afternoon in October, while leaving a community forum in her district, she made a left turn onto Riverside Avenue without fully checking the oncoming lane. The sedan came fast from her right. She heard the sound of impact before she felt anything, and then there was the body—a seventeen-year-old girl on her windshield, the sickening crumple of the collision, the girl's mother screaming from the sidewalk.

The girl survived. She spent six weeks in the hospital with a fractured femur, three broken ribs, and a traumatic brain injury that left her with lasting cognitive deficits. Margaret visited once, unable to look at the girl's face, unable to say the word "sorry" in a way that felt like anything but an insult. The girl's mother did not return her calls. The local news ran the story for three days. Margaret's political opponents called for her resignation. She did not resign, but something in her had fractured in ways that mirrors and mirrors alone could not show.

Within weeks, the physical symptoms began. When she heard raised voices—in the grocery store, in the hallway outside her office—her heart would accelerate violently, her hands would shake, and a deep ache would spread across her neck and shoulders, as though her body was bracing itself against impact. The sound of car horns made her flinch. She could not watch traffic from a window without her stomach tightening. Images of collisions would arrive unbidden: a flash of metal, a body suspended in air, the terrible physics of force meeting fragility. At night, when she tried to piece together what had happened—to understand the exact moment her attention had lapsed—the memory felt sealed off, inaccessible. She could remember the forum, the drive, the decision to turn, but the seconds just before impact were blank. Yet when the full memory did surface, usually at three in the morning, she felt the impact in her neck and shoulders as acutely as if it were happening again, a phantom echo of the collision translated into pain.

Margaret had come to believe that the accident was not an accident at all but the inevitable result of her own carelessness, her own failure to be sufficiently vigilant. She replayed the moment obsessively: she should have waited longer, looked harder, been more cautious. And more than that, she had not done enough afterward. She had not spent months in that hospital room. She had not publicly destroyed her own career as penance. She would never forgive herself for that inaction, for protecting her own life when the girl's was so damaged.

To manage the fear and the guilt, Margaret began withdrawing. She stopped driving herself anywhere, asking her assistant to chauffeur her to appointments, then gradually asking her assistant to attend meetings instead. She stopped attending community events. She stopped returning calls from colleagues. Anything that might provoke strong feeling—whether anger at a constituent, joy at a legislative victory, even the simple pleasure of a meal with a friend—felt dangerous, as though feeling anything at all might crack the careful containment she had built. She made excuses. She cited health issues. By spring, she had taken a leave of absence from her position, telling the party leadership she needed time to recover from an unspecified illness.

Her daughter, visiting from out of state, found her mother sitting in her home office in the middle of a Tuesday afternoon, having missed three consecutive committee meetings, unable to explain why. Margaret had lost weight. She had not left the house in nine days. Her neck pain was constant now, a dull throb that worsened whenever she heard a siren or saw headlights reflected in a window.

It was her daughter who finally made the call to a trauma specialist. Margaret came to the first session reluctant, convinced that talking about what happened would only make the images worse, only deepen her conviction that she was fundamentally responsible for destroying a young woman's life. But she came because her daughter had wept, and because Margaret was no longer certain she could bear the weight of staying silent.
